title: Mira and the cup of poison
hookLine: a cup of poison, and a woman who laughs as she drinks it
tomorrow: who does Mira say she belongs to?

cards: A cup is carried into a woman's room. Inside it, the song says, is poison, sent by the Rana, the head of the royal family she married into. She knows exactly what it is.
She drinks it, and she laughs. And the poison, the song says, turned to nectar. That woman is Mirabai, and the remarkable thing is who tells the story.
Not a court record. Songs sung in her voice. So who is this woman, singing about a cup of poison?

teach.b: What reaches us of Mira comes mostly through songs sung under her name and stories told about her, and tradition weaves the two together. Tradition says she was a Rajput princess who loved Krishna from girlhood.
One story: a wandering holy man gave the child a small image of Krishna, and she wouldn't let it go.
Another: watching a wedding procession, she asked her mother who her own bridegroom would be, and her mother, half joking, pointed to Krishna. Mira took her at her word.
Married into the royal house of Mewar, she kept singing and dancing in the temple among wandering sadhus, and her husband's family took it as a disgrace.

teach.h: POISON, AND A SNAKE THAT WAS A GARLAND.
teach.b: The songs tell of attempts to stop her: the cup of poison, and a basket said to hold a snake that, when she opened it, was a garland.
Through it all she sings to Krishna as Giridhar, the one who lifted the mountain, and calls him her husband, her beloved, the one she belongs to.

teach.h: A QUEEN WHO BOWED TO RAIDAS.
teach.b: Some songs in her voice even name Raidas, a saint born into a leatherworking caste, as her guru. A queen bowing to a cobbler: that's the teaching.

In bhakti, love of God outranks birth, caste and rank, and saints from every kind of family stand side by side. Other singers have sung in Mira's voice too, and some readers ask which songs go back to her.
What reaches us is still a clear voice: a woman who knows whose she is.

how: Mira bhajans are sung in homes, temples and concerts, and her life is retold in plays, films and devotional story sessions.

games.q: you're Mira. the royal house says a queen can't sing among wandering holy men of every caste. what do you do?
o: stop, and sing only in the palace temple.
keep singing with them: in bhakti, love outranks birth.
sing with them, but only the ones of royal birth.
games.why: in the songs she keeps singing among the sadhus, even when a cup of poison comes from the Rana. some songs name Raidas, a saint born into a leatherworking caste, as her guru.

practice: Mira prayed by singing. Choose one line you know, a bhajan, a name of God, even just Ram or Krishna, and hum it softly a few times, the way she sang among the sadhus, without caring how it sounds.
If you don't pray, hum any line that steadies you. Then bring to mind someone you quietly rank below you, and let them sit in the circle too.

wordCard.voice: Mirabai's songs. The songs sung in Mira's voice, of a princess who chose Krishna as her husband and kept singing when her family tried to stop her.

orig.note: Hindi, in Devanagari: the mountain-holder, Krishna who lifted Govardhan. Mira's name for him.

carryVoice: Your line: in bhakti, love outranks birth. A queen sat with wandering sadhus, and the songs remember her for it. Tomorrow: who does Mira say she belongs to?
